Keeping execution policies and perception frozen, ReWeave co-optimizes coupled context, workflows, and control loops. As new evidence revises the topology, ReWeave reprojects past trials onto the updated task understanding, exposing retained progress, regressions, and bottlenecks that guide parent selection and search width. Across tasks, matching verified local mechanisms to unmet preconditions consolidates 72 specialist units into 44 reusable groups (0.34times full concatenation) within a compact shared harness capable of continual learning. ReWeave improves held-out success from 89.00% to 98.75% on LIBERO-PRO and from 25.50% to 58.25% on RoboDojo, while uncovering retained progress in 89% of 159 failed RoboDojo development trials and translating stronger offline reasoning into higher online performance. On eight unseen LIBERO-PRO tasks, the shared harness reaches 51.3% success versus 41.3% for direct distillation, rising to 75.0% after continual learning.

nominations.title: From Rewarding What Models Say to How They Think: Attention Process Reward Model for LLM Reinforcement Learning
nominations.authors: Kairong Han, Nuanqiao Shan, Ziyu Zhao, Xinpeng Dong, Zijing Hu, Dian Jin, Leyan Deng, Junjian Ye, Lujia Pan, Fei Wu, Kun Kuang
nominations.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become an important component in large language models (LLMs). However, existing RL approaches focus on final outputs or textual solution trajectories, leading to coarse-grained rewards and unreliable reasoning. Such paradigms focus mainly on what the model outputs while overlooking how the model internally reasons. Therefore, can we reward how a model thinks internally rather than merely what it says? We first reveal the problem of textual reward aliasing in existing reward modeling approaches. Motivated by this, we propose the Attention Process Reward Model (APRM), which assigns internal rewards based on hidden states and attention maps to capture high-quality reasoning patterns. With only approximately 46M parameters, APRM is trained using ranking and counterfactual objectives, and its reward guides RL optimization while being periodically updated to handle distribution shifts. Integrated with representative RL methods, APRM achieved an average pass@8 gain of 2.88\%. Our results demonstrate the promise of incorporating internal reasoning signals into RL for LLMs.

nominations.title: NoHairCache: Calibrate-Once KV Cache Eviction with One Power-Law Exponent
nominations.authors: Shuyang Xiang
nominations.abstract: The decay exponent α in KV-cache eviction is an intrinsic property of the model: calibrated once on a single corpus, it transfers directly across domains. Attention-based accumulation (H2O) and recency-based sliding windows (StreamingLLM) are two dominant eviction frameworks, often treated as unrelated, but we show that they are the two endpoints of a single power-law family: by scoring each token as s_i = A_i cdot (t-i)^{-α}, where A_i is cumulative attention and α controls the age penalty, H2O and StreamingLLM correspond to α=0 and αtoinfty, respectively (with StreamingLLM additionally hard-coding an attention-sink patch). The no-hair mechanism of xiang2026nohair bounds the admissible range of α, and the measured exponents agree: calibrating once on WikiText yields [0.556, 0.822] for a representative model (Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct). The per-model ranges are consistent across five models (410M--1.5B) and independently match the optimal regions from perplexity sweeps. NoHairCache achieves the lowest perplexity across three datasets (WikiText, PG19, and arXiv) without per-dataset tuning, outperforming both H2O and StreamingLLM (p < 0.05 on all three datasets, with 0.06--0.10 PPL gains over StreamingLLM at budget 512). On downstream four-way multiple-choice QA, it matches or outperforms StreamingLLM across all nine (task, budget) cells, retaining 98.2% of full-cache accuracy on NarrativeQA at 25% retention versus 91.1% for StreamingLLM; per-cell McNemar tests are not significant, so QA is corroborating only. We release our calibration script and drop-in scorer upon publication.

nominations.title: The statistical analysis of complete compositional data
nominations.authors: Michael Greenacre, Ionas Erb
nominations.abstract: The analysis of compositional data is dominated by the use of Aitchison's logratio transformation; which is the logarithmic transformation of ratios of compositional features. The use of ratios was originally justified to comply with the principle of subcompositional coherence.However, there are many situations in practice where the complete composition is observed, that is, the totality of its mutually exclusive features, without the need for considering any subcompositions. In these cases, the data can be analysed on the original compositional scale, which provides a simpler and often more valid interpretation than logratios. Two real examples of complete compositional data are considered and the properties of alternative approaches to analysing them are compared. These ideas extend to some cases of incomplete compositions, where analysing them at their original scale, or normalized according to domain knowledge, is more appropriate. A Supplement includes a detailed comparison of original-scale and logratio-transformed 24-hour activity data, using a data set typical of many found in the time-use literature.

nominations.title: Conditional Independence Testing for Random Objects via Generative Models
nominations.authors: Yi Zhang, Yun Yang, Xiaofeng Shao
nominations.abstract: We propose a test of conditional independence for random objects taking values in metric spaces of negative type, allowing the conditioning variable to be either a random object or a high-dimensional vector. Our method uses multidimensional scaling and Nystr\"om extensions to obtain finite-dimensional representations of random objects from their pairwise distances, and generative neural networks to estimate conditional distributions in the embedded space. Samples from the fitted generators are then used to construct a doubly robust test statistic. Our main theoretical contribution is to quantify how errors from estimating and truncating the embeddings, together with errors in learning the conditional distributions, affect inference. We establish conditions under which these errors are asymptotically negligible, even when the embedding dimensions grow with the sample size. In particular, we derive explicit convergence rates when the conditional distributions admit generators with smooth, low-dimensional compositional structure. We establish asymptotic validity of the bootstrap test, consistency against fixed alternatives, and nontrivial power against local alternatives. Simulations with distribution-valued data demonstrate its competitive finite-sample performance.

nominations.title: Threshold Generalized Autoregressive Moving Average Models
nominations.authors: Katerine Zuniga Lastra, Airlane Pereira Alencar
nominations.abstract: Non-Gaussian time series often exhibit nonlinear dynamics and changes in dependence structures that may not be adequately captured by conventional single-regime models. To address this limitation, we introduce a class of threshold generalized autoregressive moving-average (TGARMA) models that combines observation-driven GARMA dynamics with threshold-based regime switching. The proposed framework accommodates multiple regimes, determined by a lagged endogenous or exogenous threshold variable, and allows regression coefficients, autoregressive and moving-average orders and coefficients, and, where applicable, dispersion parameters to vary across regimes. Parameters are estimated by maximum partial likelihood, while model selection is conducted using information criteria. We examine model admissibility and stability, assess model adequacy through residual diagnostics, and conduct a Monte Carlo simulation study to investigate the finite-sample performance of the estimators. The proposed methodology is illustrated using monthly counts of hospitalizations due to respiratory diseases among older adults in S\~ao Paulo, Brazil. In this application, the TGARMA model outperforms its single-regime GARMA counterpart in terms of in-sample mean squared error, highlighting the potential benefits of incorporating regime-dependent dynamics into the analysis of non-Gaussian time series.

nominations.title: Skew-Symmetric Factor Models
nominations.authors: Anna Bykhovskaya, Tomas Espana, Jianqing Fan
nominations.abstract: The paper introduces and analyzes a factor model for (real) skew-symmetric data, which arise naturally in directed flows and in pairwise comparisons used for rankings. Working within a signal-plus-noise framework, we analyze spectral inference and establish a BBP-type phase transition in signal strength. Under Gaussian noise, we derive joint eigenvalue fluctuation limits. Above the separation threshold, the estimated signal strength is asymptotically normal whenever the population strength has multiplicity one. For a general multiplicity $k$, the joint limiting fluctuations of the corresponding sample eigenvalues above the threshold are given by the eigenvalues of a scaled $k\times k$ Gaussian unitary ensemble matrix. The skew-symmetric structure induces paired eigenspaces, and we characterize the canonical angles between the population and sample eigenspaces. Below the threshold, the corresponding largest sample eigenvalue converges to the edge of the semicircle law, with fluctuations governed by the Tracy--Widom $F_2$ distribution, in contrast to the $F_1$ law familiar from real symmetric models. The approach is illustrated through financial and demographic applications.

nominations.title: Treatment Policy Design in the Presence of Measurement Error
nominations.authors: Chang Liu, AmirEmad Ghassami
nominations.abstract: In many applications, treatments are assigned based on unit features, leading to personalized treatment policies. This often involves optimizing objective functions with counterfactual quantities such as the conditional average treatment effect (CATE). In practice, some key features may be measured with error and ignoring such errors can introduce systematic bias. We study how to design personalized treatment policies when some features are latent and only noisy measurements are available. We ask how policies can be constructed when the CATE is not identifiable, and how uncertainty from measurement error can be incorporated into policy design. We propose two frameworks for treatment policy design based on partial identification, focusing on the measurement mechanism-the conditional distribution of observed measurements given unobserved features. The first framework builds on ideas from proximal causal inference. The second adopts a modular Bayesian approach based on a reparameterized likelihood, using Hamiltonian Monte Carlo and Bayesian regression models to separately perform posterior inference on the measurement mechanism and nuisance functions. Posterior quantiles are then used to construct credible intervals for the CATE that account for uncertainty in both components. Treatment policies are then derived by comparing the null value of the CATE to these bounds. The proposed methods provide a coherent way to account for measurement error and model uncertainty in personalized treatment policy design.

nominations.title: Statistical inference under response-adaptive experimental designs: a systematic review
nominations.authors: Haochen Song, Joseph Williams, Kiarash Kianidehkordi, Audrey Durand, Anna Rafferty, Tong Li, Meredith Franklin
nominations.abstract: Response-adaptive designs, including bandit-based approaches, update treatment allocation using accrued outcomes. In this paper, we systematically reviewed how studies in health and biostatistics conducted and evaluated inference under these designs. We searched six databases for studies published from January 2010 through October 2025. Of 774 records identified, 36 studies met the inclusion criteria. We summarized them using study-level counts and structured narrative comparisons, with reporting guided by PRISMA 2020. Most studies focused on methods or designs. Evidence supporting inference came mainly from theory and simulation. Among studies for which each metric was relevant, 26 of 32 numerically evaluated power, 23 of 32 type I error, eight of 35 estimator bias, and five of 12 interval coverage. These findings suggest that studies more often quantified power and type I error than estimator bias or interval coverage. Evaluations of adaptive allocation should also examine estimation and interval performance when these are relevant to the study objective.

nominations.title: A Bayesian Mechanistic Model of Spatiotemporal Dynamics in Invasive Tree Species
nominations.authors: Jiaqi Chen, Huijing Du, Yawen Guan
nominations.abstract: Modeling the spatiotemporal dynamics of invasive species requires frameworks that represent spread and growth mechanisms explicitly while accommodating the distributional features of ecological data. We propose a Bayesian mechanistic framework for invasive tree cover that combines an ecological diffusion--logistic growth partial differential equation (PDE) with a zero-inflated binomial observation model. The diffusion and growth coefficients are modeled as functions of environmental covariates, enabling direct inference on the ecological processes driving encroachment, and the zero-inflation component separates structural absence from low observed cover. To enable scalable Bayesian inference on satellite-resolution grids, we derive a homogenized equation for ecological diffusion with spatially varying diffusion and growth coefficients, which reduces computation while preserving large-scale spatial structure. Applied to satellite-derived tree cover in a subregion of the Nebraska Sandhills, where eastern redcedar is encroaching on grassland, the model indicates that elevation is strongly associated with where tree cover accumulates but only weakly with its local growth rate, whereas distance to the nearest stream is associated with both. Compared with a generalized additive model, a spatial hierarchical model fitted via INLA, and a regression tree, the proposed method directly estimates these processes as interpretable functions of environmental covariates and gives the best-calibrated predictive uncertainty.

nominations.title: When AI Performance Is Not Enough: Statistical Guardrails for Clinical Development
nominations.authors: Siddhesh Kulkarni, Gina D'Angelo, Swarna Reddy, Rakhi Kilaru
nominations.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) are reshaping the operational and inferential landscape of clinical development, yet their adoption frequently outpaces the statistical scrutiny these methods demand. This commentary offers first-principles perspectives across four application domains: anomaly detection in clinical trial data, real-time monitoring and adaptive trial designs, biomarker-based enrichment, and virtual and digital twins. For each domain, we articulate the underlying inferential problem, the contribution of AI and ML relative to established statistical methods, and the risks that statisticians, data scientists, and clinical developers must actively manage. Across these domains, a unifying theme emerges: AI and ML methods may succeed locally while failing to satisfy the broader statistical assumptions required for valid clinical and regulatory decisions. These risks include false-positive signals, compromised Type I error control in adaptive designs, conflation of prognostic with predictive biomarkers, and causal claims not supported by data and assumptions. We argue that a clearly defined context of use, relevant statistical assumptions, and consequences of the intended decision should guide the evaluation. For treatment-effect questions, the ICH E9(R1) estimand framework provides a useful organizing principle. Responsible use of AI in clinical development requires not restraint, but rigor: the inferential discipline necessary to make these technologies reproducible, interpretable, and defensible in the service of patients.

nominations.title: LEAF: Calibrated and Robust Wavelet Estimation of the Hurst Exponent
nominations.authors: Vijini Lakmini, Brani Vidakovic
nominations.abstract: Wavelet logscale regression for the Hurst exponent H of fractional Brownian motion (fBm) is sensitive to outliers and biased in finite samples. We introduce the Log-Energy with Adaptive Floor (LEAF) ordinate, which averages the logarithms of squared wavelet coefficients after adding a floor proportional to a pilot estimate of the level variance. If standardized coefficients share a common law across levels, a floor proportional to the true level variance preserves the population slope, and a consistent pilot preserves it asymptotically. We derive the asymptotic variance and influence function, and identify the variance-minimizing floor for median-pilot LEAF, whose influence grows only logarithmically. With outliers of ten increment standard deviations in up to 1% of observations, median-pilot LEAF reduces root mean squared error by a factor of 1.8 to 2.6 relative to calibrated log-energy. At H = 0.5 with 1% outliers, the error falls from 0.139 to 0.059. For small to moderate H, the main source of bias is the departure of expected wavelet energies from the ideal power law at fine scales. We estimate H from an estimating equation calibrated by simulation under fBm. Calibrating the mean logscale diagram alone delivers nearly all of the gain: it nearly eliminates bias in matched simulations and improves on the Abry--Veitch estimator most at small H. Simulations also show how scale-dependent tails can erode the gains of a robust pilot and how misspecification can undermine calibration.

nominations.title: The Curved Exponential Family of Cylindrical Distributions: m-Projection, Curvature and a Test of the von Mises-Fisher Component
nominations.authors: Amine M. Aboussalah
nominations.abstract: Cylindrical data pair a vector in R^d with a direction in S^(m-1). We study a family in which the direction is von Mises-Fisher and, given the direction, the vector is Gaussian with mean affine in it; this generalizes the Mardia-Sutton model. The family is a curved exponential family inside a regular family with Fisher-Bingham directions. We state necessary and sufficient conditions for the maximum-likelihood estimator to exist and be unique. The estimator is explicit except for one scalar root and is the m-projection (Kullback-Leibler projection) of the moment-matching member. Every moment it does not match is a function of one residual, the gap between the sample and fitted second moments of the direction. The squared length of this gap in the Fisher metric is the classical score test of von Mises-Fisher against Fisher-Bingham directions, due to Cox on the circle and extended by Mardia, Holmes and Kent. Specific here are this reading and the exact invariance of its law to the regression part. The exponential curvature lies only in the directions of the regression matrix. In closed form, the information lost on this matrix against the expected information is m-1 observations for uniform directions and (m+1)^2/(m-1) in the limit of high concentration; conditioning on the directions recovers it. Finite mixtures are identifiable. On buoy records the test rejects von Mises-Fisher directions, and generalized von Mises directions raise the held-out log-density by 0.45 nats per observation with one component.

nominations.title: Robust Forest-based Estimation of Heterogeneous Treatment Effect Under High-dimensional Confounding
nominations.authors: Zhixin Qiu, Xuanxuan Wang, Xinyuan Song, Yinfeng Wang, Yanlin Tang
nominations.abstract: Understanding how patients with Alzheimer's disease respond differently to treatment is important for individualized therapeutic assessment. Using observational data from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI), we investigate how the association between donepezil dosage and 12-month cognitive performance varies across diagnostic stages and hippocampal volumes. This analysis presents several statistical challenges, including potentially nonlinear treatment effect heterogeneity, high-dimensional confounding, and heavy-tailed outcomes with extreme observations. To address these challenges, we develop an Orthogonal Huber Random Forest (OHRF) framework that combines Huber-based robust estimation, Neyman orthogonality, and forest-based adaptive weighting. The proposed method accommodates complex treatment effect heterogeneity while reducing sensitivity to nuisance estimation errors and extreme outcomes. We establish its consistency, asymptotic normality, and finite-sample error bounds. Simulation studies demonstrate favorable estimation accuracy and robustness across a range of error distributions, particularly under heavy-tailed noise and outlier contamination. In the ADNI application, OHRF produces generally narrower pointwise confidence intervals than the conventional Orthogonal Random Forest (ORF) while revealing distinct patterns of treatment effect heterogeneity across diagnostic groups and hippocampal volumes. These findings illustrate the potential of robust, data-adaptive methods for studying heterogeneous treatment responses in complex observational biomedical data.

nominations.title: Cure-Fraction Random Survival Forests: Separating Cure from Latency
nominations.authors: Pedro Luiz Ramos, Lucas Osses, Debajyoti Sinha
nominations.abstract: In many cancer and clinical studies, the population under study has a positive fraction of long-term survivors, motivating survival models that distinguish probability of long-term survival (cure fraction) from the latency of the subgroup that is susceptible to the event. Existing survival trees and forests partition data using criteria that emphasize differences in the ranks of survival times and therefore need not identify covariates associated with cure probability. We introduce cure-fraction based survival trees (CBST) that recursively partition the covariate space using contrasts in tail survival probability supported by adequate follow-up. The resulting ensemble forest targets long-term survival heterogeneity directly rather than ranking of the survival times. We establish consistency for the induced tail-survival target and derive conditions under which our procedure consistently recovers cure-rate related partitions and cure probabilities. The analysis clarifies the separate roles of follow-up maturity, localization, and residual-tail bias in identifying cure effects and supporting statistical inference. We further develop variance estimation and asymptotic results and uncertainty quantification for predictions from the ensemble forest. Simulations show that the cure-fraction based splitting criterion can improve recovery of cure heterogeneity relative to a log-rank based forest when cure incidence and latency are driven by different covariates. Analyses of temporally held-out cohorts from the Sao Paulo Hospital Cancer Registry demonstrate that our method produces stable long-term survival risk groups while preserving substantial late follow-up support. The proposed framework provides a nonparametric approach to learning and interpreting cure heterogeneity in settings where long-term survival is the primary scientific objective.

nominations.title: Censored Regression Models with Endogeneity: A Survey
nominations.authors: Swati Shukla, Shalabh, Subhra Sankar Dhar
nominations.abstract: This survey article provides a comprehensive overview of methodologies developed to handle endogeneity in censored regression models. We emphasize their theoretical basis, and estimating methodologies. The paper summarizes the benefits and drawbacks of each technique and addresses expansions to nonlinear, panel, and high-dimensional settings, offering researchers practical assistance and identifying options for future methodological improvement in censored models with endogenous regressors.

nominations.title: Twisted Block Particle Filters: A Local Particle-System Change of Measure for High-Dimensional State-Space Models
nominations.authors: Ning Ning
nominations.abstract: Block particle filters mitigate weight degeneracy in high-dimensional state-space models, but their normalizer estimates can remain highly variable. We introduce a twisted block particle filter (TBPF) that incorporates predictive guidance through an exact change of measure at blockwise resampling. The method guide-tilts one uniformly selected offspring per block, leaves the state-transition kernel unchanged, and computes the resampling correction using finite empirical guide averages. We prove that this correction exactly preserves the finite-particle block particle filter normalizer expectation, separating the effect of guided sampling from the approximation introduced by spatial blocking. Our analysis provides exact conditional local moments and a one-step conditional central limit result. We further derive explicit bounds on the correction accumulated across blocks and time, establish fixed-horizon consistency of the block filter and corrected normalizer under suitable regularity and guide-range conditions, and identify conditional criteria for guide perturbations that reduce variance. Experiments on coupled linear Gaussian and stochastic-volatility models with up to 256 latent dimensions show lower measured log-normalizer variance. For stochastic volatility with a five-step guide, the median reduction is $38\%$. An application to a 100-dimensional financial portfolio panel extends the evaluation to real data.

nominations.title: Correlation-aware sequential sampling for multi-output polynomial chaos expansions
nominations.authors: Qitian Lu, Miroslav Vo\v{r}echovsk\'y, Luk\'a\v{s} Nov\'ak
nominations.abstract: The interaction of multiple physical processes in complex engineering systems is often characterized by several quantities of interest (QoIs) with non-negligible cross-correlations. Accurate uncertainty quantification of these responses requires repeated model evaluations, which can be computationally expensive. As an alternative, polynomial chaos expansion (PCE) provides an efficient surrogate modeling framework for reducing this computational cost owing to its natural structure for statistical analysis, while adaptive sequential sampling can further improve sampling efficiency under a limited model evaluation budget. However, adaptive sampling strategies specifically designed for multi-output PCE remain limited, and existing approaches commonly aggregate information from individual outputs without explicitly accounting for their statistical dependence. When strong correlations exist among QoIs, output-wise aggregation can give greater combined influence to response patterns shared by several outputs. To reduce the influence of such repeated representation on sample allocation, this study develops a principal component analysis-based extension of the multi-output criterion for adaptive construction of PCE. The sampling criterion combines component-wise normalization with the retention of selected principal directions, thereby adjusting the relative influence of shared response patterns while preserving distance-based exploration. The method is verified through numerical examples with different levels of output coupling and is compared with the conventional multi-output criterion and reference sampling strategies. The results demonstrate that accounting for output dependence improves the allocation of new samples among multiple response features and enhances the efficiency of multi-output PCE surrogate construction, particularly for strongly correlated QoIs.

nominations.title: Adaptive Two-Sample Testing for Regression Discrepancy and Model Misspecification in High Dimensions
nominations.authors: Yu Peng, Jiaqi Huang, Falong Tan, Lixing Zhu
nominations.abstract: In two-sample regression comparisons, testing for equality is often too restrictive because minor discrepancies in functional form are unavoidable in practice. We study whether the functional discrepancy falls within a practically acceptable tolerance. Such tolerance-based comparison can, however, be unreliable when either regression model is misspecified. To address both issues, we propose a unified adaptive-to-model testing framework for high-dimensional regressions that integrates model checking with functional similarity testing for the two populations. For functional similarity, we develop an adaptive boundary-proxy test whose rejection probability converges to the nominal level at every fixed configuration of the composite null hypothesis, overcoming the conservatism of conventional least favorable configuration tests. For model misspecification, we use projection-based tests for sparse high-dimensional regression models. These components are combined through adaptive gating into a joint test. We investigate its asymptotic null distribution and power properties under global and local alternatives. Numerical studies examine its finite-sample performance.

nominations.title: ATLAS: Autoregressive Trajectories for Longitudinal Analysis of Survival
nominations.authors: Morgan Nissen, Chunyang Li, Seth Glazier, Julia Bohman, Ahmad Halwani, Jeffrey Humpherys
nominations.abstract: Dynamic survival prediction requires estimates that reflect a patient's observed clinical history. We introduce ATLAS (Autoregressive Trajectories for Longitudinal Analysis of Survival), a framework that trains a sequence model on longitudinal data and autoregressively samples possible futures conditional on an individual's covariates and observed history. These trajectories form a patient-specific synthetic cohort from which Kaplan-Meier survival curves and Aalen-Johansen cumulative incidence curves are estimated. We evaluate ATLAS using two stochastic finite-state automaton benchmarks with exact conditional reference curves: a single-covariate process with duration dependence and a late rule change, and a three-covariate Markov process with recovery and competing causes of death. Comparisons include eight direct survival models, including validation-optimized DRSA and Dynamic-DeepHit and history-aware SurvTRACE adaptations, with each neural model trained nine times in the first experiment and five times in the second. After baseline, every ATLAS configuration had lower mean survival-curve error than every fitted direct comparator in both experiments. With a common Sobol sampler and 10,000 trajectories per patient, the best ATLAS model did so in every individual training run, and its mean error was 62% to 84% lower than that of the strongest direct comparator. Baseline advantages were smaller and less consistent in the duration-dependent experiment. ATLAS provides a generative framework for history-conditioned survival estimation, while the accompanying benchmarks enable direct assessment of individual survival and competing-risk predictions against known reference curves.

nominations.title: Model Selection and Averaging: Signal Strength, Ordering, and Oracle Risks
nominations.authors: Guangyuan Cui, Yuhong Yang
nominations.abstract: Existing oracle risk comparisons of model selection (MS) and model averaging (MA) have primarily distinguished slowly and rapidly decaying ordered signal-importance sequences, leaving the comparison beyond these idealized but practically unrepresentative decay conditions insufficiently characterized. We revisit this problem for a complete nested collection of linear regression models with independent homoscedastic errors. Without prescribing a coefficient decay pattern, we establish necessary and sufficient conditions for the relative oracle gain of MA over MS to be asymptotically substantial or negligible. Under complete ordering of the coefficients, the determining quantity is the share of oracle MS risk contributed by components near the noise level. This characterization explains how the strengths and numbers of strong, moderate, and weak signals jointly affect the comparison. Under an arbitrary fixed ordering, a common pool-adjacent-violators partition represents both oracle risks and yields an analogous characterization through block averages and sizes. For application, we develop a consistent diagnostic under sub-Gaussian errors and suitable growth conditions, together with finite-sample confidence intervals under Gaussian errors. The Gaussian framework also provides confidence sets for a certain Rashomon set. Simulations and a diamond-price application illustrate the theoretical findings and the empirical assessment of the potential MA advantage.

nominations.title: Why flattening the P-value histogram works: a theory of the standard-deviation optimization in tensor-decomposition-based unsupervised feature extraction
nominations.authors: Y-h. Taguchi, Turki Turki
nominations.abstract: Background: Tensor-decomposition-based unsupervised feature extraction (TD-based UFE) selects genes by attributing P-values to the components of a gene singular vector under a null normal distribution. The standard deviation sigma of this distribution is unknown and is chosen so that the histogram of the P-values of the genes that are not selected becomes as flat as possible. This heuristic has worked well in practice but has had no theoretical justification. Results: We prove, for a model of signal, mean expression and noise, that the higher-order singular value decomposition has a component that reproduces the experimental design, that the components of its gene singular vector belonging to background genes are approximately normal with standard deviation sigma_0 = sqrt(d)/s, where d is the noise variance and s the singular value, and that signal genes separate from the background even when they form a positive fraction of all genes. We derive the limit of the objective function of the flattening and prove, by a computer-assisted argument based on interval arithmetic, that for 100 histogram bins, Benjamini-Hochberg level 0.01 and every fraction of background genes between 0.1 and 0.99, the limit has a unique minimizer within 1.1% of sigma_0. We formalize the practice of taking the valley to the right of the peak of the objective as a maximum-drop rule and prove that the resulting estimator is consistent up to this bounded bias. Conclusions: Flattening the P-value histogram estimates the noise level of the background genes, with a small and bounded systematic bias, provided that the signals are strong enough to be detected individually and that the noise variances of background genes are nearly equal.

nominations.title: Deep Negative Binomial Autoregression for Sparse Spatio-Temporal Counts: Estimation and Predictive Distribution Bounds
nominations.authors: Hsin-Hsiung Huang
nominations.abstract: We study estimation and probabilistic forecasting for sparse, overdispersed count panels using DeepNB-STAR, a negative binomial autoregression whose log-mean and log-size are outputs of a deep ReLU network of temporal and neighboring summaries of the past, fitted by maximum likelihood. We prove an oracle inequality for the Hellinger risk along the observed trajectory without mixing assumptions, rates governed by compositional smoothness with a matching lower bound for a H\"older subclass, geometric absolute regularity, and bounds on the error of h-step predictive distributions of order h^{1/2} times the root estimation risk plus a Monte Carlo term. All results hold for a size that depends on the covariates, and the estimation bounds hold under arbitrary dependence between sites, with the number of time points as sample size. On four Japanese surveillance panels, DeepNB-STAR has a weighted interval score 0.6% to 1.0% below that of a three-member ensemble of Temporal Fusion Transformers on every panel, distinguishable from zero only on the held-out panel. Fitted mean and size functions are reported with exploratory bootstrap intervals. Nominal 95% prediction intervals for national totals cover only 81% to 92% of weeks: the joint predictive law, unlike the estimator, relies on conditional independence across sites.

nominations.title: The minimax value of outcome feedback in budget-constrained adaptive sampling
nominations.authors: Shengye Tao
nominations.abstract: Whether adaptivity improves estimation is a classical question in sequential design and information-based complexity. In practice, adaptive data collection can use two different kinds of information: process data on whether each contact succeeded, and the observed outcomes themselves. How much each kind is worth in the worst case under a hard budget has not been settled. We study this question for estimating a common Bernoulli mean through channels with unknown response probabilities and known costs, where failed contacts are charged and the budget must hold on every sample path. We compare static designs, designs that adapt to response indicators only, and fully adaptive designs, each with an arbitrary estimator. Our main theorem shows that when the costs are invariant under a group of channel permutations acting transitively on the nuisance parameter, outcome-adaptive allocation has zero minimax value: response-adaptive and fully adaptive designs have the same minimax risk, given by a one-dimensional optimization and attained by an explicit least-favourable prior and equalizer rule. For two contacts we obtain a closed-form criterion for when response feedback strictly improves on every static design. An unequal-cost example with a computer-certified exact saddle shows that the same conclusion can hold without symmetry, even though no product prior is least favourable there. A correlated prior shows that outcome feedback can still reduce Bayes risk, so the equivalence is genuinely minimax. In this idealized setting, the results support responsive survey designs that adapt to paradata but not to outcomes.

nominations.title: Tuning the false discovery rate in the closed eBH procedure
nominations.authors: Vladimir Vovk
nominations.abstract: The closed eBH procedure controls the false discovery rate under arbitrary dependence between the input e-values. It takes the target false discovery rate $\alpha$ as its input and outputs a rejection set $R$, the usual goal being to maximize its size $\left|R\right|$. This note discusses a modification of the closed eBH procedure that allows choosing the target false discovery rate post hoc: the rejection set and its level $\alpha$ can be chosen after seeing the data, and the expected ratio of the false discovery proportion to $\alpha$ is at most 1. We adapt Vovk and Wang's (2023) algorithm for computing discovery e-matrices to computing, in quadratic time, the frontier of achievable combinations $(\left|R\right|,\alpha)$ of the size of a rejection set $R$ and its level $\alpha$. The frontier allows us to compute an optimal rejection set in view of a given utility function $F$, $F(\left|R\right|,\alpha)\to\max$, striking a balance between the goals of reducing $\alpha$ and increasing $\left|R\right|$.

nominations.title: Nonparametric estimation of a common marginal hazard function under censoring and spatio-temporal dependence
nominations.authors: Ibrahim Loudy, Kowir Pambo Bello, St\'ephane Bouka, Guy Martial Nkiet
nominations.abstract: This article investigates the nonparametric estimation of a common pooled marginal hazard function from right-censored durations exhibiting spatio-temporal dependence. We propose two estimators based respectively on the Nadaraya-Watson method and the (k)-nearest neighbors (k)-NN) approach. Under assumptions of stationarity, regularity, non-informative censoring, and weak spatio-temporal dependence, we establish their pointwise and uniform convergence rates as well as their optimal asymptotic order. A simulation study compares their finite-sample performance. Two real-data applications with right censoring are considered: a multicenter clinical trial with 53.8 percent censoring and 1,746 geolocated and time-stamped requests submitted to New York City's 311 municipal service, of which 35.5 percent are censored. The empirical results illustrate the relevance of the proposed methods in the presence of spatial and temporal dependence.

nominations.title: Limit theorems for almost conditionally identically distributed random variables
nominations.authors: Marco Battiston, Lorenzo Cappello
nominations.abstract: $\xi$-Almost Conditional Identically Distributed ($\xi$-a.c.i.d.) random variables are generalizations of conditional identically distributed (c.i.d.) and exchangeable ones. $\xi$-a.c.i.d. random variables arise naturally in applications in statistics, such as in recursive algorithms and heteroskedastic observations, and are parametrized by a sequence $\xi=(\xi_{n})_{n\geq 0}$ that quantifies departure from the c.i.d. property. In this work, we extend limit theorems for exchangeable and c.i.d. random variables to the more general setting of $\xi$-a.c.i.d. random variables. After proving a Strong Law of Large Numbers, we provide necessary and sufficient conditions for the asymptotic directing measure of the sequence to be absolutely continuous with respect to a given $\sigma$-finite measure. Then, under regularity assumptions on the parameter $\xi$, three different Central Limit Theorems for $\xi$-a.c.i.d. sequences are derived, involving the predictive, empirical and asymptotic directing distributions. These theorems have several statistical applications, including the construction of asymptotic credible intervals in Bayesian predictive inference.

nominations.title: Sub-Gaussian HDLSS Principal Component Analysis: High-Probability Theory and Numerical Evidence for NRM, CDM, and Block Noise Reduction
nominations.authors: Yugo Nakayama
nominations.abstract: We study principal component analysis when the dimension d is much larger than the sample size n under an independent-factor sub-Gaussian model. The dual sample covariance is decomposed into a finite-rank score matrix, an isotropic bulk shift, and a high-probability remainder governed by the bulk trace \tau_0, Frobenius scale q_0, and largest noise eigenvalue b_0 = ||\Lambda_0||_{op}. This decomposition separates fixed-score HDLSS limits from joint limits in which n also grows. It shows that sequential noise reduction generally targets a score oracle containing a later-spike subtraction, while an oracle block correction avoids that subtraction when the signal rank is known. A parallel cross-data-matrix bound explains the benefit and cost of sample splitting. Reproducible Gaussian-factor simulations with 1,000 replications per configuration confirm the score-oracle approximation, the multi-spike subtraction, the separation between eigenvalue and eigenvector scales, and the population transition when n grows.

nominations.title: The broken-sample problem revisited II: Detecting hidden linear dependencies
nominations.authors: Shuyang Gong, Yihong Wu, Jiaming Xu
nominations.abstract: We study the detection problem for shuffled linear regression, in which the covariates and the responses are either independent or linearly related through a latent correspondence. Consider independent standard Gaussian covariates \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\in\mathbb R^d\) and scalar responses \(Y_1,\ldots,Y_n\). In a shuffled linear model, \(Y_i=\langle X_{\pi_*(i)},\beta_*\rangle+\sigma Z_i\), where both the permutation \(\pi_*\) and the regression coefficient $\beta_*$ are latent and $Z_i$'s are white Gaussian noise. The goal is to distinguish this model from one in which the covariates and responses are independent with the same marginal distribution. In the low-dimensional regime of $d \ll \frac{\log n}{\log\log n}$, we show that the detection threshold is given by $\sigma=o(1)$ for fixed $d$ and $\sigma^2 = \Theta(\frac{1}{d\log d})$ for growing $d$; both thresholds are achieved in nearly linear time using moment-based test statistics inspired by matched filters in signal processing. For higher dimensions, tests based on sliced Wasserstein distance succeed when $\sigma^2 = o(\frac{1}{(d\log d)^2})$, while the optimal threshold remains open. As a by-product, we show that the shuffled linear model exhibits an ``all-or-nothing'' phase transition for estimating $\beta_*$ at $\sigma^2\asymp \frac{1}{d\log d}$ in low dimensions. In particular, $\beta_*$ can be consistently estimated in nearly linear time, even when it is information-theoretically impossible to recover any positive fraction of the latent matching $\pi^*$.

nominations.title: A high-dimensional perspective of assortative mating: definition, dynamics, and limiting results
nominations.authors: K\'ari Hlynsson
nominations.abstract: Assortative mating, or the systematic (dis)similarity of traits between mate pairs, has wide-ranging consequences. Chiefly, it modulates genetic variance in offspring due to the coupling of inherited trait-associated loci in parents. Over many generations, this buildup becomes appreciable at the trait level and may confound statistical genetics techniques, such as association analyses and heritability estimation. Theoretical characterisations of this effect are well-developed in the univariate case, where mates assort on a single trait pair. However, empirical studies increasingly show that assortment is not only multivariate, but high-dimensional, in that the correlation structure exhibited between mates cannot be represented by a single or few linear combinations of the constituent traits. In spite of this, the mathematical theory of assortment has not scaled with awareness of this fact. In this paper such a generalisation is developed. We begin by deriving sufficient conditions under which an estimator is invariant to assortment, followed by studying existence conditions and limiting behaviour of equilibria under assortment. Finally, univariate results involving trait heritability and consanguineal genetic correlation are generalised to the multivariate regime.

nominations.title: Sharp Asymptotic Theory of Maximum Likelihood Estimation for Gaussian Processes with a Matern Kernel
nominations.authors: Ameer Qaqish, Sudipto Banerjee, Didong Li
nominations.abstract: Gaussian processes (GPs) provide a flexible framework for modeling complex dependence structures through a covariance function, or kernel, whose parameters determine the variability, correlation, and smoothness of the underlying process. The Mat\'ern kernel is among the most popular choices due to its flexibility in modeling different degrees of smoothness. Although the identifiability of Mat\'ern kernel parameters under fixed-domain asymptotics is completely understood, identifiability alone does not establish the consistency or asymptotic behavior of the maximum likelihood estimators (MLEs) routinely used in practice. In this paper, we address this gap by developing a sharp asymptotic theory for the joint MLE of Mat\'ern kernel parameters. Since parameter identifiability depends critically on the dimension of the observation domain, we characterize the estimable parameters and establish their convergence rates across different dimensions. We establish joint asymptotic normality and minimax optimality of the convergence rates. In addition, we establish asymptotically valid confidence regions for the estimable parameters. Our results accommodate irregular sampling designs and extend to sub-Gaussian measurement errors. Extensive simulation studies illustrate the theoretical results.

nominations.title: How long must an honest confidence interval be after causal discovery? Benign and malignant weak edges
nominations.authors: Ruiqi Zhao
nominations.abstract: After causal discovery, a confidence interval for a total effect valid uniformly over the model class must pay for structural uncertainty. We measure this price by the worst-case ratio of expected length to that of the efficient interval knowing the graph, for linear Gaussian models with a known superset of the adjacencies and k-triangle faithfulness. The global price is of order sqrt(n) once one edge can be malignant, so we study it locally, near a generic distribution with one edge absent. Our main result classifies this weak edge by Meek closures. It is benign if deleting it leaves the effect identifiable in the resulting MPDAG and Markov equivalent explanations agree; the local price is then bounded, and otherwise, for small k, of order sqrt(n). At benign edges the price is of order R+K, with R a ratio of efficient lengths and K a cross-model constant. It equals one, so that honesty is free, exactly when K = 0, generically decided by a d-separation. For two Markov classes it is determined within a factor 3.40, and its upper bound is approached without knowing the base point or the weak edge. A further graphical condition gives the rate uniformly in a second edge's margin.

nominations.title: Measuring Colombia's Informal Output: Relative Earnings and Identification in a Bayesian Two-Sector Model, 1993-2026
nominations.authors: Jaime Vera-Jaramillo
nominations.abstract: How much of Colombia's measured output is produced by informal work? The answer cannot be read from the labor-informality rate: Colombia combines an informality rate above 50% with a much smaller informal share of output, because informal work is less productive. We estimate a Bayesian two-sector business-cycle model on quarterly national accounts and on reconstructed employment and informality series for 1993-2026. Identification comes from a new quarterly series of informal-to-formal labor earnings built from household-survey microdata for 2007-2026. Formal production uses capital and labor, informal production is labor based, and an accounting relationship maps relative earnings, the informality rate and the formal capital share into the informal output share. We show that aggregate data alone cannot pin down the size of the informal sector, and that relative earnings identify its quarterly path: from 2007 the path is invariant, within 0.3 percentage points, to the model's steady state. The informal share declines from about 30% of GDP in 1993 to 20% in 2026Q2, while labor informality falls from about 69% to 54%. The estimates lie within the range of published shadow-economy series for Colombia, close to the enhanced MIMIC estimates of Asllani, Dell'Anno and Schneider for 2009-2020. Sensitivity analysis quantifies the role of the capital share and of non-wage labor costs.

nominations.title: Decision Theory with Degree of Membership in the State Space
nominations.authors: Jeff Dominitz, Charles F. Manski
nominations.abstract: Classical decision theory considers a decision maker (DM) who faces a choice set C and believes that the true state of nature s* lies in a state space S. An objective function w(., .): C x S -> R1 maps actions and states into welfare. The DM wants to maximize w(., s*) but does not know s*. The state space specifies a labeled set of possible states. Possibility is binary: every state in S is possible and no state outside of S is possible. Thinking that this binary perspective on possibility is too rigid, we generalize the classical theory. We begin with a universe of labeled states U and a residual unlabeled state r. Classical theory associates a binary possibility indicator mu(s) with each s in (U, r). The residual state r is not possible, so mu(r) = 0. The state space is S = [s in U: mu(s) = 1]. We expand the range of mu to be the interval [0, 1]. Thus, mu is now a real number measuring degree of membership, a term we adopt from fuzzy set theory. The membership function mu(.): (U, r) -> [0, 1] differs substantively from but is consistent with the subjective probability distributions of Bayesian decision theory. Bayesian theory places a subjective distribution on the elements of a classical state space, each of whose members has degree of membership one. Degree of membership expresses the distinct idea that a DM may want to quantitatively express uncertainty regarding the composition of the state space. A mathematical distinction between subjective probabilities and degrees of membership is that the former must sum to one, but the latter need not. After formalizing basic ideas, we extend three prominent classical decision criteria--maximization of subjective expected welfare, minimax regret, and maximin--to our generalization of classical decision theory.

nominations.title: Quadratic Forms of Multivariate $t$-Distributions
nominations.authors: Brendan Kline
nominations.abstract: This paper concerns quadratic forms of multivariate $t$-distributions. This paper derives the joint distribution and density of multiple quadratic forms, and establishes the possibility of a finite series approximation to the CDF. The paper also provides closed-form expressions for all the mixed moments that exist. Inverses of quadratic forms and ratios of quadratic forms are also considered.

nominations.title: Probability-Feasible Historical Transport: Sharp Bounds and Falsification Tests for Distributional Pre-Trend Designs
nominations.authors: Ulrich Hounyo
nominations.abstract: Distributional difference-in-differences studies often assume that the post-policy gap between treated and comparison groups is a mixture of pre-policy gaps. This historical-transport assumption can fail in ways that one-statistic checks miss. When policy events are pooled, the average counterfactual can be a valid distribution although no event's counterfactual is, and pooled bounds can exclude the true average effect. Mixtures of past gaps can assign negative probability to outcomes, and cutoff-by-cutoff bounds can be incompatible. We characterize sharp bounds and give breakdown radii, a grid-free confidence region, and tests with and without an experiment. The tests reject transport in the National Supported Work data and expose impossible state counterfactuals behind a pooled minimum-wage bound. For the 1993 Earned Income Tax Credit expansion they pass through 1995, when bounds put single mothers' employment gain relative to childless women at 5 to 7 points; the gain stays positive after dropping early welfare-waiver states.

nominations.title: Sharpe Ratio Inference after Machine Learning
nominations.authors: Sander Barendse, Ming Cheng
nominations.abstract: The economic value of return signals is often assessed using the Sharpe ratios of portfolios based on those signals. In modern asset pricing, return signals often depend on many features, including state variables and firm-specific characteristics, and machine-learning methods are increasingly used to estimate them. But how much confidence can we place in the estimated Sharpe ratios? We find that signal-estimation error can remain consequential for inference even in large asset panels. Moreover, pooling observations across assets does not necessarily make this uncertainty negligible when predictors contain common features or exhibit substantial cross-sectional dependence. As a remedy, we develop a debiased Sharpe-ratio estimator that accounts for signal-estimation error and provides valid confidence intervals and tests against benchmarks. Our target is the population Sharpe ratio of a specified portfolio rule evaluated at the true conditional expected returns given the features. The framework covers market-timing, long-short, and other signal-based portfolios, allowing the number of assets to grow with and greatly exceed the time-series sample size. The method combines orthogonal portfolio moments with time-series cross-fitting and remains valid under suitable estimation-error bounds for machine-learning forecasts. Empirically, we revisit the setting of Gu et al. (2020) using machine-learning estimators of the return signals. The strongest long-short Sharpe-ratio gains relative to market benchmarks remain significant after debiasing, providing statistical evidence of the economic value of their feature set. Conventional and debiased Sharpe-ratio estimates are generally similar, while the associated confidence intervals and tests can differ substantially. These differences vary across signal estimators and portfolio rules and do not uniformly weaken the evidence of portfolio performance.

nominations.title: Shadow economy as a null set. Measure-theoretic approach to shadow economy
nominations.authors: Rados\l{}aw A. Kycia, Andrzej Buszko
nominations.abstract: In this paper we asked if the shadow economy can be defined as a system of null sets for institutional measures or sensors that measure economic transactions. As an answer a measure-theoretic testable framework to redefine and quantify the shadow economy was designed. Traditional economic definitions frequently conflate the actual shadow economy with the observational limitations of state institutions. To resolve this, we model the shadow economy as a null set relative to institutional measures and analyze three complementary economic regimes. We explore in this context how standard mathematical tools can be given economic meaning. First, in the low-resolution regime, we apply Banach Lattices and Lebesgue decomposition of a measure to address transaction underreporting by aggregating incomplete institutional registries using a supremum fusion operator. Second, for hidden economic dimensions, we utilize Copula theory and Kullback-Leibler divergence optimization to reconstruct unobserved financial flows from technological and physical indicators. Third, we address audit scalability by modeling the shadow economy as a sparse vector, applying Compressed Sensing to detect high-volume sparse evasion networks through random, incoherent, and privacy-preserving sampling.

nominations.title: The Entangled Veil: Why Redistribution Requires a New Language
nominations.authors: Nazaria Solferino, Viviana Solferino
nominations.abstract: The Rawlsian veil of ignorance requires choosing principles of justice without knowing which position-temporal, spatial, social, or personal one will occupy. We argue that this object cannot be represented faithfully within standard economic models. A faithful representation must satisfy three requirements: it must treat all generations symmetrically, capture non-separable correlations among positions, and allow mobility costs to vary across locations and occupations. We show that standard optimal-tax models violate at least one requirement, and that the minimal framework satisfying all three is a geometric framework adapted from string theory, in which the veil is an entangled state over a space of possible life situations. We derive full equalization as a first-best benchmark, the emergence of separated clusters when correlations reward distinction, a symmetry between intraand inter-generational equity, and a tunneling mechanism by which correlations reduce institutional barriers. The model generates four inequality profiles and four inequality types. The estimates are quantitatively important: the framework changes the ranking of redistributive policies, and ignoring the margins it identifies leads to systematically biased policy evaluation.

nominations.title: Adaptive experiments with observational data: Efficient experimental design and asymptotic time-uniform inference for long-term treatment effects
nominations.authors: Kentaro Kawato
nominations.abstract: Estimating long-term treatment effects in experiments requires waiting for outcomes to become observable, which can delay both the evaluation of an intervention and subsequent decisions. Recent econometric work has developed identification methods that combine experimental data with observational data containing long-term outcomes. This paper proposes using observational data available before the experiment begins not only for identification but also for designing adaptive experiments, in which experimental data are collected sequentially. To estimate the long-term average treatment effect as precisely as possible, we express its semiparametric efficiency bound as a function of the covariate sampling and treatment assignment rules and minimize the bound over these rules to characterize an optimal fixed experimental design. This experimental design depends on the treatment-specific conditional variances of the observational prediction of the long-term outcome, which can be learned only from experimental participants. We therefore construct a sequential procedure that learns the experimental design as experimental data accumulate and show that its estimator attains the same limiting variance as an oracle estimator implemented under the optimal fixed experimental design. We further construct an asymptotic confidence sequence whose coverage holds simultaneously over all rounds after a prespecified start, so that the experimenter can inspect the interval after each participant and stop once it excludes zero. Monte Carlo simulations show that the learned experimental design can improve precision and shorten the time to detection relative to baseline sampling and equal-probability assignment. An illustration using the Pakistan Graduation experiment shows how estimated conditional variance heterogeneity informs sampling and treatment assignment.

nominations.title: What Should an Experiment Measure? Combining a Short-Term Experiment with Confounded Observational Data to Identify Long-Term Treatment Effects
nominations.authors: Kentaro Kawato
nominations.abstract: Observational data often record long-term outcomes but do not identify long-term treatment effects when selection depends on unrecorded characteristics, while randomized experiments remove this selection but require years of follow-up. We ask what a short-term experiment should measure so that, combined with observational data, it identifies the average long-term treatment effect in the observational population. In our main setting, the observational data record a coarse post-treatment measurement of the unrecorded characteristics but not a detailed measurement that would remove confounding. In this setting, we derive three implications for what the experiment should measure. It should (1) collect the same coarse measurement, (2) measure the characteristics in enough detail that conditioning on this detailed measurement and recorded covariates removes confounding and leaves the coarse measurement uninformative about selection and the treatment-specific long-term outcome mean, and (3) distinguish no more levels of the characteristics than the coarse measurement can separate. We characterize the treatment effect through linear inverse problems based on exclusion restrictions and completeness, and thereby show that combining such an experiment with the observational data identifies the effect. We propose an estimator that is based on the efficient influence function and removes the first-order effect of nuisance estimation errors. We give conditions under which this estimator is asymptotically normal and attains the semiparametric efficiency bound. Cross-fitting relaxes the conditions on nuisance estimation. In simulations and a Job Corps illustration, the proposed Tikhonov-penalized series estimator has smaller absolute bias and coverage closer to the nominal level than competing estimators.

nominations.title: Spurious Information in Large Markets: Random Matrix Laws for Entropy, Mutual Information and the Value of Information
nominations.authors: James Rice
nominations.abstract: Entropy, Kullback-Leibler divergence and mutual information have become standard currencies for measuring how much one set of financial variables reveals about another. In large cross-sections they are almost always computed from sample covariance matrices, and the noise in those matrices is the object of random matrix theory. This paper develops the random matrix theory of Gaussian information functionals and applies it to markets. I show that the plug-in mutual information between two blocks of p and r variables estimated from $n$ observations has an exact expected excess, the spurious information, that is a digamma telescope independent of the true dependence. Under independence its law is that of a product of Beta variables. In the proportional regime it grows linearly with an order-one variance. The same quantity is a linear spectral statistic of the Jacobi ensemble, which yields a closed form for the logarithmic moment of Wachter's law. Spurious information increases strictly whenever uninformative coordinates are added. In a CARA-Gaussian economy the certainty-equivalent value of a signal equals mutual information divided by risk aversion, so these results translate one for one into a spurious value of information. The canonical-correlation phase transition then defines a frontier of minimum detectable information. On daily returns of 49 US industry portfolios from 1990 to 2026, I document the market mode, the reliability of sector eigenvectors implied by the BBP transition, the out-of-sample cost of noise dressing, and an information linkage between carbon-intensive and financial industries that survives exact bias correction and conditioning on the market.

nominations.title: Growth versus equity in a stochastic multiplicative wealth model: The cost of redistribution and the emergence of an inequality Laffer curve
nominations.authors: Renato Vieira dos Santos
nominations.abstract: A stochastic multiplicative wealth model with taxation and redistribution is extended to include two channels through which fiscal policy can reduce the economy's average growth rate: productive disincentive (a tax-dependent mean return) and administrative inefficiency (loss of part of the collected revenue). For uniform redistribution, the stationary density of normalized wealth remains an inverse-gamma law, but its shape parameter acquires a richer dependence on the tax rate. The central finding is the emergence of an "inequality Laffer curve": when the disincentive is sufficiently strong, the Gini coefficient first decreases, reaches a minimum at a finite tax rate, and then increases again as taxation intensifies. In the extreme limit the stationary state collapses back to the condensed phase, restoring the oligarchic transition. Both channels also create a direct trade-off between inequality and long-run average wealth, giving rise to a welfare-maximizing tax rate. The two channels are combined into a single analytically tractable model, and all predictions are validated by agent-based simulations. The results show that the qualitative existence of an optimal tax rate is robust whenever the aggregate growth rate responds to fiscal policy, while the inequality Laffer curve is a specific prediction of the productive-disincentive channel.

nominations.title: Echoes of the boom in hydraulic fracturing: What changes in Louisiana's energy complex reveal about global energy cycles
nominations.authors: Alexander S. Kolker, Robert Habans, Trey Cowan
nominations.abstract: The expansion of hydraulic fracturing (i.e. fracking) led to global shifts in energy markets that were felt acutely along the US Gulf Coast and particularly in the state of Louisiana. This article presents a data-focused examination of trends in the energy industry, and shows how they led to potentially counterintuitive, negative impacts in Louisiana's economy. Most notably, hydraulic fracturing led to a massive expansion in oil and gas supplies that contributed to a significant decline in oil prices in late 2014, contributing to significant job losses. Louisiana's economic downturns were tied to global shifts in energy markets that had major geostrategic implications. More broadly, results indicate that large and long period cycles in the supply, demand and price of oil can have widespread impacts on job creation and loss. In states like Louisiana with a large and diversified energy complex, the impacts of these trends can be highly uneven. One impact in the 21st Century appears to be highly concentrated areas of industrial development within a broader pattern of regional economic decline. Furthermore, trends identified in this study suggest the potential for the emergence of major cycles in the gas market. Whereas natural gas was previously mostly transported by pipelines and sold through long-term contracts, the emergence of liquified natural gas creates the potential for more volatile gas market dynamics. The implications of gas market cycles, while not yet known, could be of major economic significance.

nominations.title: What the annual energy balance hides: the coordination value of digital platforms for positive energy districts
nominations.authors: Arega Getaneh Abate, Per Sieverts Nielsen, Xiufeng Liu, Brian O'Regan, Gerfried Cebrat, Cigdem Karadag, Valentina Zaccaria, Yang Liu, Madalin Silion, Ami Vadiee, Jakob Jespersen, Mahmut Sami Buker, Maria Simona Raboaca, Avinash Renuke, Betul Erdor Turk, Dudle Stewart
nominations.abstract: Positive energy districts (PEDs) are usually assessed by annual net energy, whereas distribution networks operate hour by hour. An annually positive district still imports on low-generation hours and exports or curtails on high-generation hours. How large this hourly imbalance is behind an annual balance, and how much of it coordination among prosumers can close without new physical capacity, is not established. This paper models a multi-carrier prosumer community coupling electricity and heat behind a shared grid connection with a net-export hosting limit. The model is solved as a centralized community problem and as a price-taking peer-to-peer (P2P) market. Under convexity, the equilibrium implements the regularized community optimum and the P2P and congestion prices are the duals of the pool-clearing and hosting constraints. The model is calibrated to six European district archetypes with constructed hourly profiles. Hourly self-sufficiency is only 48-50% in the four deeply studied districts and ranges from 48-55% across all six, leaving a no-platform coordination gap of 2.8-5.9% of no-platform economic cost. The shared-forecast step recovers only 6-18% of the gap, while grid-aware pricing reduces curtailment by 45% in the primary district. Coordination mainly reduces surplus-side inefficiency, whereas closing the deficit side requires storage. The results are scenario-based projections for calibrated archetypes, and the operating benefit is small and contingent on binding hosting limits and high feed-in remuneration. For regulators and distribution system operators this supports hourly, bidirectional indicators alongside the annual positive-energy target, and a congestion charge active only in binding hours with a predetermined refund, while the business case for a platform at district scale rests on grid-side value and aggregation across districts.

nominations.title: How to Mismatch Consumers
nominations.authors: Wenhao Li
nominations.abstract: Should a platform show all consumers all products, or at least those they like most? Or could it raise consumer surplus by mismatching some consumers: showing them only less-preferred products or even excluding them from trade? I show that in both monopoly and duopoly, mismatching can raise aggregate consumer surplus by inducing lower prices. In duopoly, consumer-optimal matching uses a cutoff policy: along each diagonal of equal valuation differences, consumers with lower valuations are matched only to less-preferred products, and some may subsequently be excluded. With independent uniform valuations, this raises aggregate consumer surplus by about 41% over full matching.

nominations.title: Neighbourhood flood damage amplifies mortgage default cascades
nominations.authors: Matteo Valle, Drona Kandhai, Cees Diks, Debraj Roy
nominations.abstract: Floods threaten mortgage repayment by damaging homes, disrupting incomes, and worsening conditions in surrounding neighbourhoods. However, it remains unclear how these neighbourhood effects turn local damage into systemic mortgage distress, as Europe's housing crisis leaves households that lose their homes with few affordable alternatives. Using an agent-based model calibrated to Limburg, the Netherlands, we show that damage to surrounding properties can trigger mortgage defaults among households that can still afford to pay, including those whose own homes remain undamaged. In the most severe flood scenario, the annual foreclosure rate more than doubles. As each foreclosure lowers the value of nearby homes, it triggers a cascade. Floods make such large foreclosure cascades more frequent, with the share of foreclosures that belong to these cascades rising from 31% to 45%. They also shift foreclosures towards younger mortgages, when more debt is still outstanding. These findings show how neighbourhood damage extends mortgage risk beyond directly flooded homes and causes foreclosures to arrive in concentrated waves earlier in repayment.

nominations.title: Do Candlestick Charts Suffice? The Incremental Economic Value of Technical Indicators in Stock Return Prediction
nominations.authors: Peng Liu, Yanyan Zheng
nominations.abstract: Although technical analysis remains widely used in practice, the need for manually constructed indicators is increasingly questioned as deep learning models can extract features directly from OHLC price data. This paper examines the standalone economic value of trading volume and manually constructed technical-indicator groups and whether adding these groups to OHLC candlestick charts provides incremental economic value. Using daily data for 1,707 Chinese A-share stocks from 2013 to 2025, we construct approximately 3.36 million stock-window samples and encode them as multi-channel images containing candlestick charts, trading volume, and seven widely used manually constructed technical indicators. The primary analysis uses a 2D CNN on these images; complementary tests apply a logistic regression, a 1D CNN, and an LSTM to numerical representations of the same samples. Out-of-sample performance from 2021 to 2025 is evaluated using decile portfolios, Sharpe ratios, Fama--French alphas, and formal pairwise tests. Our empirical results yield two central findings. First, specifications based separately on OHLC, trading volume, and each technical-indicator group produce significantly positive high-minus-low returns and factor-adjusted alphas, together with economically meaningful Sharpe ratios; the OHLC-only specifications generally perform best under the nonlinear models. Second, adding these technical-indicator groups to OHLC does not systematically improve any of these performance measures in our setting. Together, these results provide the first large-scale evidence from the Chinese A-share market on the standalone and incremental economic value of these technical-indicator groups across multiple representations and model architectures.

nominations.title: The Private Production of Safety Outside Options and the Burden of Protection
nominations.authors: Elena Pisanelli
nominations.abstract: Protective interventions are typically evaluated by their ability to prevent harm. Yet protection also raises a distinct question: who bears the burden of adjusting to violence? I examine this allocation of protective adjustment using four randomized interventions in the United States. An offer of permanent housing assistance increases separation from a baseline partner combined with stable independent housing by 12.52 percentage points. Assignment to active police-response protocols reduces observed victim-only departures and increases suspect-only departures. Assignment to an emergency protection order increases documented directions for suspects to leave. These findings reveal two margins of the same allocation problem: housing assistance expands victims' ability to establish an independent residence, while enforcement shifts displacement obligations toward suspects. Protective policies thus shape not only the opportunities for safety, but also the distribution of the costs required to achieve it.

nominations.title: AI-Assisted Programming and Labor Demand
nominations.authors: Lindsey Raymond, Eleanor Wiske Dillon
nominations.abstract: Generative AI has demonstrated human-level performance on technical work tasks, yet evidence on how these task-level capabilities are changing labor demand remains scarce. We study the firm-level adoption of GitHub Copilot, an AI coding assistant, across 5,414 multinational firms accounting for 38% of the U.S. programming workforce. To identify causal effects, we exploit a natural experiment generated by firms' predetermined software procurement cycles. Early AI-adopting firms hired more workers before the launch of GitHub Copilot and had larger, more technical, and older workforces. After one year, GitHub Copilot adoption reduces quarterly technical hiring by 29% among review-induced adopters, with no effect on separations, overall technical headcount, or vacancy duration. The hiring slowdown is concentrated in the subset of junior technical roles that involve the highest share of coding work. Overall, AI coding assistance causes firms to shift demand towards more experienced workers and roles that pair some coding with broader design responsibilities.

nominations.title: Place-Based Policy from Space: Evidence from Italy's Inner Areas
nominations.authors: Nicola Caravaggio, Giuseppe Di Renzo, Giuliano Resce, Agapito Emanuele Santangelo, Giulia Valeria Sonzogno
nominations.abstract: This paper evaluates a place-based policy, Italy's National Strategy for Inner Areas (SNAI), using satellite nighttime lights. Targeting structurally fragile and peripheral municipalities, SNAI invests in essential services and economic activities. Staggered difference-in-differences compares 941 funded municipalities with 3,112 eligible controls over 2011--2022. Funding is associated with an expansion of lit area and no detectable change in radiance per lit cell, suggesting that activity extends its footprint rather than intensifying in existing centres. The expansion holds across comparison groups and, descriptively, concentrates at intermediate funding per resident. Annual satellite data can complement slower and coarser statistics.

nominations.title: Topological Pharmacokinetics: A Model-Free Framework for Quantifying the Shape of Concentration-Time Curves
nominations.authors: Hong-Can Ren, Ya-Xin Gu
nominations.abstract: Pharmacokinetic analysis compresses concentration-time curves into scalar summaries (non-compartmental analysis, NCA) or pre-specified compartmental models, approaches that are either model-free but shape-blind or shape-sensitive but structure-dependent. We introduce Topological Pharmacokinetics (TPK), a framework that reads curve shape directly from data without committing to any model. TPK delay-embeds each curve into a state-space trajectory and applies persistent homology to extract a nine-component topological invariant: multi-scale shape descriptors (peak hierarchy, secondary-peak isolation, loop structure) with established perturbation-stability properties. We evaluate the framework on four layers of increasing realism. Monophasic linear systems generate no spurious cyclic signals, whereas double-site absorption and enterohepatic recirculation produce distinct loop signatures; 12 nonlinear scenarios resolve as curvature-without-cycles; a weak endogenous rhythm survives superposition with a large exogenous drug signal (inter-peak interval recovered at exactly 24 h); and loop detection stays stable to 10 percent of Cmax additive noise and to sampling thinned to 7 points.
